title: Role-Based Access Control
summary: Role-based access control (RBAC) is an access control model in which permissions are assigned to roles rather than directly to users, and users receive permissions only through the roles granted to them. The model is usually decomposed into users, roles, permissions, operations and objects, with role hierarchies allowing a senior role to inherit the permissions of a junior one and constraints preventing conflicting combinations from being held simultaneously. In practice RBAC is the default model for Active Directory groups, Linux groups, Kubernetes role bindings, cloud IAM policies and nearly every commercial application, and it succeeds or fails on the quality of role design rather than on the model itself. Roles that accumulate permissions over years, roles that are granted for convenience rather than function, and role explosion where hundreds of near-duplicate roles exist because exceptions were encoded as new roles rather than handled as exceptions, all produce effective privilege that far exceeds intent. Role mining and periodic recertification are the corrective processes: derive candidate roles from observed entitlement usage, consolidate what overlaps, and require an accountable owner to affirm every assignment on a schedule. The persistent gap is that RBAC answers whether a subject holds a permission but not whether the request is appropriate for the moment, which is why organisations layer attribute-based or context-based conditions over role assignment for sensitive operations. Segregation of duties and least privilege are both expressed through RBAC, so careful attention to role-to-permission mapping and to the aggregation of inherited roles is where real assurance comes from.
objectives: You will be able to model users, roles, permissions and role hierarchies for a representative application.
You will be able to explain how role inheritance and the aggregation of multiple roles produce unintended effective privilege.
You will be able to run role mining and recertification to consolidate role explosion and remove unused entitlements.
You will be able to design segregation-of-duties constraints that keep conflicting duties out of one identity.
You will be able to review cloud IAM policies and Kubernetes role bindings for overly permissive or wildcard grants.
You will be able to explain the limits of RBAC for context-sensitive decisions and when to add attribute-based conditions.

beginner.definition: Role-based access control, or RBAC, gives permissions to roles instead of to people. A role is a job-shaped bundle of rights, such as help desk agent or finance approver. You get rights only through the roles assigned to you.
beginner.whyItMatters: Assigning rights one person at a time does not scale, and it hides mistakes. Roles make access easier to review and to remove when someone changes jobs. But roles also rot. They collect extra permissions over years, and people keep roles they no longer need. Regular review is what keeps the model honest.
howItWorks: You list the permissions your applications support, such as read, write, and delete.
You group related permissions into roles that match real job duties.
You then assign people to whole roles instead of to single permissions.
A senior role may inherit the permissions of a junior role, which saves effort.
You review the assignments on a schedule and remove what is no longer needed.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital. Nobody gives a new doctor a list of individual permissions on their first day. Instead, the doctor joins the physician group, which already carries the usual rights. A cleaner joins a different group with a different set. Changing jobs means changing groups. The group list is short enough to check.
takeaways: You should give permissions to roles, and then give roles to people.
Roles grow over time, so review every assignment on a schedule.
Many roles together can grant more than any single role suggests.

exercises.title: Role-Based Access Control - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Role-Based Access Control - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: Role-Based Access Control - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: Role-Based Access Control - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.
